explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Luke 10:1 says Jesus sent them “…two by two…” so every traveler had a partner. Nobody was walking those roads alone. I think a buddy beside you sounds nice, especially when you need somebody to hold the map.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Luke 10:1 says the Lord sent them two by two ahead of Him. Seventy-two people, so that's thirty-six pairs heading out. Nobody had to talk to himself the whole way.

explanations.answer: Ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Jesus says, “Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest.” Look at what He tells them to do first. He doesn't say go recruit or panic. He says ask.

explanations.answer: Hire more workers from the towns nearby
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a sensible plan, baker, but Jesus doesn't say it. He says to ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers. The seventy-two aren't told to run a hiring drive. I've seen people try to fix a short staff by just making a bigger sign, and it never goes the way they hope.

explanations.answer: Let the field rest until next season
explanations.explanation: Close to a farmer's instinct, friend, but not what Jesus says. He says the harvest is plentiful, and then He tells them to ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers. Nothing in His words puts the field on hold. This harvest is ready now, and my dough doesn't wait for next season either.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Go! I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.” He tells them plainly what they're walking into. I'd have asked for the whole job description twice.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Jesus does say it, friend. In Luke 10:3 He tells them, “Go! I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.” That's the picture He gives them as they head out. It's a heavy line, so it's worth a second read.

explanations.answer: A purse or bag or sandals
explanations.explanation: Right, friend! Jesus says, “Carry no purse or bag or sandals.” That's a short packing list, and it's a short one. Imagine the stares at the front door of the first house.

explanations.answer: A staff or cloak or tunic
explanations.explanation: That's a decent travel list, baker, but it's not the one Jesus gives. In Luke 10:4 He names a purse, a bag and sandals. A staff, a cloak and a tunic aren't mentioned in that verse. It's an easy mix-up when you're packing in your head.

explanations.answer: A lamp or scroll or blanket
explanations.explanation: Good guesses for a trip, friend, but Jesus doesn't name those. He says, “Carry no purse or bag or sandals.” Lamp, scroll and blanket never come up in the verse. If I were packing, I'd be arguing with myself over the blanket.

explanations.answer: It returns to them
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “If a man of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; if not, it will return to you.” So the peace isn't tossed out the window. It comes back to the ones who said it.

explanations.answer: It stays on the house anyway
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd lean that way, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. He says, “If a man of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; if not, it will return to you.” With no man of peace in the house, the peace comes back to the seventy-two. It doesn't stay behind.

explanations.answer: It's lost for good
explanations.explanation: Nothing gets lost here, baker. Jesus says, “if not, it will return to you.” The peace comes back to the ones who spoke it. I wish every dropped cookie came back to me that politely.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. In Luke 10:7 Jesus says, “Stay at the same house, eating and drinking whatever you are offered.” Then He adds, “Do not move around from house to house.” So where they're welcomed is where they settle in. No house-hopping.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around, baker. Jesus says, “Stay at the same house… Do not move around from house to house.” So they stay put where they're welcomed. The text doesn't give them a house tour.

explanations.answer: Heal the sick and tell them God's kingdom is near
explanations.explanation: Right, baker! Jesus says, “Heal the sick who are there and tell them, ‘The kingdom of God is near you.’” One thing to do and one thing to say, both in the same verse. They get to eat what's set before them, and then they get to bring healing and good news to the table.

explanations.answer: Teach the law and settle all their disputes
explanations.explanation: That's a big job, friend, and it's not the one Jesus gives here. In Luke 10:9 He sends them to heal the sick and to tell the people that the kingdom of God is near them. Teaching the law and settling disputes aren't part of that verse. Those folks already have enough on their plates.

explanations.answer: Gather the people and collect an offering
explanations.explanation: No offering plate in this verse, baker. Jesus says, “Heal the sick who are there and tell them, ‘The kingdom of God is near you.’” That's the assignment: heal and tell. Collecting isn't in it.

explanations.answer: The dust of the town clinging to their feet
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Jesus says, “Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet, we wipe off as a testimony against you.” It's a message you can see, down to the dust on their feet. And right after that comes the line, “Yet be sure of this: The kingdom of God is near.”

explanations.answer: The water of the town's well from their hands
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but no wells in this one. Jesus says the dust of the town that clings to their feet is what they wipe off. Water on hands isn't mentioned anywhere in the verse. The feet are doing all the work here.

explanations.answer: The ashes of the town's fires from their cloaks
explanations.explanation: Ashes do show up in this passage, friend, just not here. In Luke 10:13 they're in the line about sitting in sackcloth and ashes. For the unwelcoming town, Jesus says to wipe off the dust that clings to their feet. Cloaks don't get mentioned.

explanations.answer: repented
explanations.explanation: That's the word, baker! Jesus says those cities “…would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.” He says Tyre and Sidon would have done it. Chorazin and Bethsaida had the miracles performed in them, so His words to them are heavy.

explanations.answer: rebelled
explanations.explanation: I get the pull of that one, friend, but it isn't what Jesus says. He says Tyre and Sidon “…would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.” Rebelled is a different word from repented. Repented is the one in the verse.

explanations.answer: rejoiced
explanations.explanation: That's a happy word, baker, and it's not what Jesus says. He says they “…would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.” Sackcloth and ashes is a sorrowful picture. It's about turning back, not celebrating.

explanations.answer: It will be brought down to Hades
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus says, “And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!” He asks the question and then answers it Himself. It's a heavy word for a town, so I'll just say it plainly and let it sit.

explanations.answer: It will be handed over to its enemies
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a thing that happens to towns, baker, but Jesus doesn't say it. He asks if Capernaum will be lifted up to heaven and answers, “No, you will be brought down to Hades!” Enemies never come up in the verse. It's one of those heavy lines, and the text stays right on it.

explanations.answer: It will be left in ruins forever
explanations.explanation: Close in mood, friend, but not in words. Jesus says, “No, you will be brought down to Hades!” The word ruins isn't in that verse. When a line is this heavy, I'd rather stay with exactly what He said.

explanations.answer: The One who sent Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! Jesus says, “Whoever listens to you listens to Me; whoever rejects you rejects Me; and whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me.” It's a chain with three links. The seventy-two carry His message, so how people treat them lines up with how they treat Him.

explanations.answer: The prophets before Him
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, friend, but Jesus doesn't say it here. In Luke 10:16 the chain ends with “…the One who sent Me.” The prophets don't appear in this verse. The last link is the One who sent Him.

explanations.answer: Moses and the law
explanations.explanation: Good name to reach for, baker, but it's not in this verse. Jesus says, “…whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me.” Moses and the law aren't in that sentence. The chain stops at the One who sent Him.

explanations.answer: Even the demons submit to them in His name
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! They say, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name.” Notice the last part, in His name. They come back with a report and they point to who it's about.

explanations.answer: The dead were raised in every town
explanations.explanation: Big claim, baker, but it's not what they report. In Luke 10:17 they say, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name.” Nothing there about raising the dead in every town. The text keeps the report to the demons.

explanations.answer: Fire fell from heaven at their word
explanations.explanation: Dramatic, friend, but that's not their report. They say, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name.” Fire from heaven isn't in the verse. I'd have loved to see the demons submitting, though.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Luke 10:17 says, “The seventy-two returned with joy…” Joy is how the text says they came back, and it doesn't say they were discouraged. Then they tell Jesus, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name.”

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The text says, “The seventy-two returned with joy…” That's how they walk back in. Jesus then answers what they report, so you can tell they were bursting with it.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Behold, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will harm you.” That's a big gift, and it comes from Him. They're not carrying it on their own.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Jesus does say it, friend. In Luke 10:19 He tells them, “Behold, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.” He says He has given it to them, and then adds, “Nothing will harm you.” So this one is True.

explanations.answer: That their names are written in heaven
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend! Jesus says, “…do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The demons submitting was big news, and He still points them to something bigger. Their names are written in heaven.

explanations.answer: That every town will remember them
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, baker, but it's not what Jesus says. He says, “…rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” Being remembered by towns isn't in the verse. The place their names are written is heaven.

explanations.answer: That they will see greater miracles
explanations.explanation: That sounds exciting, friend, but Jesus doesn't promise it here. He says, “…do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” Greater miracles aren't in the verse. He turns their joy to their names in heaven.

explanations.answer: little children
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Jesus says, “…You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children.” He says it while rejoicing in the Holy Spirit. And He adds, “Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight.”

explanations.answer: the priests
explanations.explanation: Reasonable guess, friend, but that's not who Jesus names. He says the Father has revealed these things “…to little children.” Priests aren't in that verse. The wise and learned are the ones He says it's hidden from.

explanations.answer: the rulers
explanations.explanation: Not the rulers, baker. In Luke 10:21 Jesus says the Father has hidden these things from the wise and learned and “…revealed them to little children.” Rulers don't come up in that line. Little children are the ones who get it.

explanations.answer: Those the Son chooses to reveal Him to
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Jesus says, “…no one knows who the Father is except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.” So knowing the Father comes through the Son. It's something He gives.

explanations.answer: Those who study the law most closely
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a reasonable path, baker, but Jesus doesn't say it. He says, “…no one knows who the Father is except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.” Studying the law isn't mentioned in this verse. It comes down to those the Son chooses.

explanations.answer: Those who keep every single commandment
explanations.explanation: Hang on, friend, that's not in this verse. Jesus says, “…those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.” Keeping every commandment isn't the condition He names. Even I would be nervous if that were the test.

explanations.answer: Many prophets and kings
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Jesus says, “…many prophets and kings desired to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.” That's a lot of important people who wanted what the disciples had. They were standing right in front of it.

explanations.answer: Many priests and scribes
explanations.explanation: Good try, friend, but Jesus names someone else. In Luke 10:24 He says it was “…many prophets and kings…” who desired to see and hear what the disciples did. Priests and scribes aren't in that verse. It's the prophets and kings.

explanations.answer: Many judges and elders
explanations.explanation: Close in sound, baker, but not what Jesus says. He says “…many prophets and kings desired to see what you see but did not see it…” Judges and elders aren't mentioned there. The ones He names are prophets and kings.
